idiom_name: concurrent.futures Executor.submit() as the dispatch step (ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work)
implementation_notes: concurrent.futures supplies the dispatcher and the performer pool in one object: Executor.submit() hands exactly one callable to one pooled worker, map() batches the same hand-off, and shutdown()/the context manager define the drain contract; ThreadPoolExecutor is the performer pool, ProcessPoolExecutor is the same interface with real parallelism for CPU-bound work, and multiprocessing.Pool offers the same shape with apply_async. The asyncio form swaps the executor for asyncio.Queue() plus N create_task() consumers, which is the only variant with real back-pressure built in. Write your own dispatcher loop only when the selection rule needs message inspection; the executor itself has no routing and no priorities.
code_sketch:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8, thread_name_prefix="performer") as pool:
    for msg in channel:
        pool.submit(handle, msg)      # one performer per message, bounded pool

# asyncio equivalent with back-pressure:
# queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=64)
# [asyncio.create_task(worker(queue)) for _ in range(8)]
# await queue.put(msg)               # producer blocks when performers lag
pitfalls: submit() never blocks and the work queue is unbounded, so overload is invisible until memory runs out; bound it with a semaphore or use asyncio.Queue(maxsize=...).
An exception inside a submitted callable is stored in the Future and only re-raised when result() is called; fire-and-forget submission silently swallows failures.
Threads cannot speed up CPU-bound work under the GIL - use ProcessPoolExecutor - and processes pay pickling for every argument and result, so large objects must be passed by reference or by file.

ThreadPoolExecutor threads are joined at interpreter exit and should not be used for long-running tasks (documented): a hung performer blocks shutdown, and shutdown(wait=False) still leaves the pool's threads running.
Mutable arguments and pooled workers interact badly: a worker function that closes over mutable state shares it across all performers.
